w5c.title: Retained
w5c.summary: Milo, dead mid-complaint on a Tuesday, is handed a laminated org chart by Prava, who tells him his skills are a strong culture fit. For the first time in decades he feels useful, and he accepts Reconciliations before anyone offers him a choice. The afterlife now has his consent.

w5c.title: Lanyard, Desk, Mentor
w5c.summary: Milo is issued a lanyard and a desk facing Zara's across a low partition and pitches himself as a hit-the-ground-running person. Zara answers with flat instructions: close what is in your queue and open nothing else. He takes her courtesy for friendship, while she has started to size him up.

w5c.title: Nobody Reads the Appendices
w5c.summary: Over the gray coffee, Old Fen remarks without looking up that nobody reads the appendices, which is what they are for, and Milo hears about tenure, quotas and the quarter's single graduation. He laughs, filing it away as office lore. The reader learns the rules are hidden in plain sight while Milo stays happily incurious.

w5c.title: Four Minutes
w5c.summary: Halvard Bell's account arrives restructured, and Milo zeroes the tenure and initials the form in under four minutes. Bell's desk is cleared before the coffee finishes dispensing. When Milo asks where Bell goes, Zara tells him to write 'under' and nothing else. That night, uneasy, he locks the ledger in his drawer without knowing why.

w5c.title: The Memo
w5c.summary: A heavy memo signed by Edric Thane summons Milo, who reads it as a promising career signal. Zara tells him plainly it is not normal: bring nothing, sign nothing, and if offered a chair, stand. For the first time Milo has been warned, and the danger is now real to him.

w5c.title: Appetite
w5c.summary: In the cold corner office Milo stays standing, and Edric Thane, hands folded on a closed ledger, calls his four minutes appetite rather than diligence and tells him he was hired for not asking questions, which is not why he will be kept. The Lich has noticed Milo, and Milo leaves knowing it.

w5c.title: Moved
w5c.summary: Milo unlocks his drawer and finds, in a column no one ever explained to him, that Bell's tenure was moved, not zeroed. He brings the discrepancy to Zara. She looks at it for a long time, tells him he has finally read an appendix, and sits him down for paperwork. Milo has crossed from not asking to knowing.

w5c.title: Grief Ink
w5c.summary: After hours, Zara shows Milo the parts of the contract printed in ink that appears only under grief, and Bell's form reveals clauses he signed off without seeing. Milo learns the paperwork he trusted has a second layer. Zara's flat training reads, for the first time, as deliberate.

w5c.title: Tie-Out
w5c.summary: Milo does what he is best at and reconciles account after closed account. Every 'zeroed' balance has moved into the same column, and tenure is vanishing faster than labour can explain. His pleasure in the pattern curdles once he sees how big it is.

w5c.title: Top of the Org Chart
w5c.summary: The column ends in a single pooled account with Edric Thane's name on it. Milo understands that the souls sent under are not destroyed but harvested to keep the CEL continuing, and that this is the business, with everything else as overhead. Zara admits she has known for a hundred years. Milo can no longer claim not to know.

w5c.title: The Onward
w5c.summary: Milo asks why the Lich, if graduation is real, never took it. Zara says Edric Thane chose continuance over the onward because he is afraid of it, and that this fear is the crack in him. The villain stops looking all-powerful and starts looking like a clerk who never left.

w5c.title: Process Improvement
w5c.summary: Milo drafts a crisp report proposing to streamline the harvest, with throughput metrics he is proud of, and pictures the Lich calling him interesting again. Zara reads it without comment and hands it back. Milo has become the Edric of six hundred years ago, and part of him knows it.

w5c.title: Confetti That Never Lands
w5c.summary: At the all-hands, the quarter's single graduation is celebrated with dissolving confetti. Afterwards Milo finds Prava weeping off the clock over a private ledger of eleven thousand names. The harvest stops being numbers and becomes the people Prava remembers.

w5c.title: Filed Himself
w5c.summary: In Records, Milo watches Old Fen, content and filing himself away, and envies him. Then he sees the envy for what it is: the same wish not to ask that made Milo useful to the Pipeline. He cannot submit the report.

w5c.title: Signature Sheet
w5c.summary: Milo tears up his report in front of Zara. She lays out what she has built toward for two centuries: not a rebellion but a union of the dead and a work stoppage done entirely as procedurally impeccable paperwork. Milo signs first. The act turns: the clerk has chosen the harder way.

w5c.title: One Signature at a Time
w5c.summary: Milo follows Zara through Retention and Records as she gathers signatures, never louder than a form. Even Old Fen signs, slowly, in his best filing hand. Alone, the dead had no leverage. Now they have a list, and Milo sees that organising is its own kind of ledger.

w5c.title: Eleven Thousand Names
w5c.summary: The official ledger has erased the identities of the souls sent under, and Milo's reconciliation stalls. Prava brings him her forbidden private ledger with every name she ever onboarded. Her grief becomes evidence, and the reconciliation becomes possible.

w5c.title: Restructuring Request
w5c.summary: Milo reconciles every account the Pipeline has sent under, restoring each soul's tenure line by line, and the totals point back to one pooled account. With Zara he fills out the restructuring of Edric Thane's account on the department's own standard form and files it through Reconciliations. The Lich is now a case in Milo's queue.

w5c.title: Reply All
w5c.summary: Zara sends the work stoppage as an all-staff email that is, for once, completely honest, and the Marrow District stops hoping on schedule. A memo summons Milo to the quarterly review. There is no going back.

w5c.title: Do Sit
w5c.summary: Edric Thane offers a chair again and Milo stands again, this time on purpose. The Lich treats the stoppage as a negotiation he has already won. Milo is no longer the eager hire. He is the auditor in the room.

w5c.title: A Single Sheet
w5c.summary: Milo hands over his resignation with the reconciliation attached: every harvested soul's tenure restored and the pooled account zeroed under the rules Edric enforced for six centuries. Edric reads it to the last appendix and finds no error. The clerk has been undone by a clerk.

w5c.title: Filed Correctly
w5c.summary: Edric admits he never took the onward because he was afraid of it. Then he initials the reconciliation in the box marked for it, files it correctly and goes onward. The Lich ends by his own terms of service, and the office returns Milo changed.

w5c.title: Plain Language
w5c.summary: Back in Reconciliations, the Pipeline has to explain to its customers in plain language what it does. Milo, bored again, understands his boredom was never a personality but a wound where his questions used to be. Zara, across the partition, finally has company.

w5bc.title: A Meeting That Could Have Been an Email
w5bc.summary: Milo dies mid-sentence, complaining about a pointless meeting, and the forty-one years of comfortable, unquestioned optimisation he took for a personality end without ceremony; he is no longer alive, but still, faintly, waiting to be told what to do.

w5bc.title: Retained
w5bc.summary: Prava slides a laminated org chart across a laminate desk and tells Milo, warmly, that he has been retained as a strong culture fit; the first person ever to call his boredom valuable wins his yes before a choice is offered, and he files away, without asking, that she used his name before he gave it.

w5bc.title: Lanyard, Desk, Mentor
w5bc.summary: Orientation issues Milo a lanyard and a vocabulary in which 'restructured', 'under' and 'the CEL' mean nothing in particular, and he decides the CEL must be a department; he arrives at his desk in Reconciliations eager to be useful, and the first thing he learns there is what it feels like to be politely unseen.

w5bc.title: Sometimes It's Quieter
w5bc.summary: Zara Okafor, his desk neighbour and trainer, answers Milo's run-on, eager questions in three words or fewer and never looks up; Milo mistakes her flat courtesy for the start of a friendship, and the reader sees that she is assessing him.

w5bc.title: Zero It Out
w5bc.summary: Zara drills Milo in the procedure for closing a restructured account: review the remaining tenure, zero it, initial, send under, and never ask where under is; Milo masters it faster than anyone she has trained, and discovers, uneasily and then happily, that he likes being good at it.

w5bc.title: Confetti That Dissolves
w5bc.summary: At the all-hands in the bedrock amphitheatre the quarter's single graduation is celebrated and the newsletter praises Reconciliations' closure rate, with Milo's numbers singled out; feeling seen for the first time in two lives, he commits fully to the job, while Zara, beside him, watches the confetti vanish before it lands.

w5bc.title: Nobody Reads the Appendices
w5bc.summary: Sent to fetch a contract from Records, Milo meets Old Fen, content and half-filed himself, who tells him without looking up that nobody reads the appendices; Milo envies the old man's peace and laughs the line off, but it lodges.

w5bc.title: Halvard Bell Does Not Reconcile
w5bc.summary: Closing the file of Halvard Bell, a former dentist with ninety years in Retention whose contract was restructured at nine that morning, Milo finds that Bell's tenure is gone before it was zeroed, more than his labour could explain; for the first time he does not file it, and asks Zara where it went, and she looks up.

w5bc.title: Go to Records
w5bc.summary: Zara will not tell Milo where Halvard Bell's tenure went; she gives him a file number and two words, 'Go. Read.', and he leaves his desk on an errand he does not yet realise is a test, his question now officially open.

w5bc.title: Ink That Shows Under Grief
w5bc.summary: Old Fen, contentedly filing, hands Milo the full contract and the appendices printed in ink that only appears under grief; Milo, remembering Halvard Bell, can suddenly read them, and learns that 'sent under' means transferred, not closed, while Fen's serene refusal to care becomes both the thing Milo envies and the thing he begins to fear.

w5bc.title: The Account at the Top
w5bc.summary: Running the numbers end to end with the gusto of a man finally given an interesting problem, Milo follows every restructured soul's tenure up the org chart into a single pooled account held by the CEL, and understands at last that the CEL is not a department but Edric Thane, the Chief Executive Lich, kept continuing on harvested hope.

w5bc.title: A Discrepancy Worth Escalating
w5bc.summary: Milo's first instinct is to optimise: he drafts a crisp report to Management flagging the leakage as a process inefficiency, imagining recognition and a promotion; Zara reads it over the partition, says nothing, and lets him send it, leaving him to sit alone with what he has just chosen.

w5bc.title: Eleven Thousand Names
w5bc.summary: Off the clock, Prava shows Milo the private ledger she is not permitted to keep, every soul she has onboarded, his own name and Halvard Bell's among them; the leakage in his report becomes people, and his pride in it turns to shame.

w5bc.title: Summons
w5bc.summary: A memo arrives: the CEL would like a word regarding Mr. Voss's report; Zara, still not looking up, tells him only to read everything before he signs anything, and Milo realises that his report has already reached the one reader who matters.

w5bc.title: The Corner Office
w5bc.summary: Edric Thane, formal and thorough, commends Mr. Voss's diligence, admits he was once a clerk who reconciled exactly as Milo does, and offers him a path upward into Management and eventually into continuance; Milo is tempted, until a question the Lich cannot answer plainly about the onward shows him that Edric Thane stayed because he is afraid of what graduation actually is.

w5bc.title: I'm In
w5bc.summary: Milo politely declines the offer and walks back down to his desk, where he tells Zara, in a long hedging sentence that is nonetheless a commitment, that he wants to join whatever she is building; she looks up, and the recruitment she has run for a year becomes a union of two.

w5bc.title: One Line Per Soul
w5bc.summary: Milo starts the reconciliation of every soul ever sent under with the first line he can bear to write, Halvard Bell's, and Prava gives him her forbidden ledger so that each line can carry a name rather than a number; the project stops being an audit and becomes an act of restitution, and Milo finds himself asking questions again, out loud.

w5bc.title: Sign Here
w5bc.summary: Zara carries a signature sheet through the Marrow District, to the Retention team, cheerful and despairing, who sign in tears that look like smiles, and finally to Old Fen, who reads the appendices for the first time in centuries and, to Milo's surprise, signs; contentment cracks into solidarity, and the dead are no longer alone.

w5bc.title: Restructuring Request
w5bc.summary: Milo and Zara fill out a standard restructuring form, in triplicate and without a single error, for the account of Edric Thane, and file it through Reconciliations, the department built to close accounts; the Lich's own procedure is now the instrument pointed at him, and it cannot be withdrawn.

w5bc.title: Reply All
w5bc.summary: Zara lets Milo press send on an all-staff email announcing the work stoppage in plain language, what the Pipeline pipes, where, and to whom; the Marrow District goes quiet, quieter than Zara has ever heard it, and a summons to the quarterly review arrives within the minute.

w5bc.title: A Single Sheet
w5bc.summary: In the corner office Milo hands Edric Thane his resignation with the reconciliation attached; the Lich reviews it line by line, looking for the error a clerk always leaves, and finds none, and for the first time in six centuries his numbers belong to someone else.

w5bc.title: Filed Correctly
w5bc.summary: Edric Thane acknowledges, with a clerk's terrible courtesy, that the restructuring is in order, initials it in the box marked INITIAL HERE, and as his pooled account zeroes out and the tenure flows back to its owners he goes onward, toward the thing he feared; Milo watches him go and understands they were the same man once, and are not any longer.

w5bc.title: Plain Language
w5bc.summary: Aeon Holdings issues its first plain-language notice to its customers explaining exactly what it does; at intake, Prava reads the names in her ledger aloud as their tenure returns, and weeps on the clock for once, because leaving is real.

w5bc.title: Company
w5bc.summary: Back at his desk with nothing urgent to do, Milo feels his old boredom return and recognises it at last not as a personality but as the wound where his questions used to be; he asks Zara whether it is always this quiet, and she looks up, answers, and stays, and two centuries of anger give way to company.

w5bd.title: A Meeting That Could Have Been an Email
w5bd.summary: Milo dies mid-sentence on a Tuesday, still complaining about a pointless meeting, and opens his eyes in a gray atrium with a numbered ticket in his hand. His first reaction is not grief but a mild, familiar sense that there must be a process, and that he will be good at it.

w5bd.title: Retained
w5bd.summary: Prava slides a laminated org chart across a laminate desk and tells Milo, warmly, that he has been retained and is a strong culture fit for Reconciliations. Milo, who has never been told his boredom was valuable, says yes before anyone offers him a choice, and Prava writes his name somewhere he cannot see.

w5bd.title: Sometimes It's Quieter
w5bd.summary: In the windowless Marrow District, Milo is given a lanyard, a desk and a trainer, Zara Okafor, who teaches him tenure, quotas and the one graduation per quarter in short flat sentences and never looks up. He mistakes her courtesy for friendship; she, without saying so, starts measuring him.

w5bd.title: Sent Under
w5bd.summary: Zara walks him through his first closure: review the remaining tenure, zero it, file the form that sends the soul under. Milo asks, eagerly, where under is, and Zara says it is not on the form; he decides that is fine, and the deciding is the first thing he is good at.

w5bd.title: Top of the Curve
w5bd.summary: Milo leads the department in closures and is congratulated in the newsletter, and the praise feels like being seen. Zara, without comment, starts handing him the harder files and asking him one small question about each, which he answers cheerfully and then cannot stop thinking about.

w5bd.title: The File of Halvard Bell
w5bd.summary: Milo opens the account of Halvard Bell, a dentist who spent ninety years in Retention and was restructured at nine that morning. For the first time a closure has a face and a career attached, and Milo, reading it more carefully than the quota requires, finds he is slower than usual.

w5bd.title: It Doesn't Reconcile
w5bd.summary: Halvard's ninety years of tenure do not add up to the balance Milo is meant to zero; the difference has already left, flowing upward into a single pooled account at the top of the org chart. Milo turns to tell Zara as if he has found a bug; she does not look up, says 'Again,' and makes him run the numbers until he understands it is not a bug, ending the act with the discrepancy his and no longer deniable.

w5bd.title: Records
w5bd.summary: Milo goes down to Records to request the pooled account's history and finds Old Fen, so long in the stacks he has begun to file himself, who hands over the right drawer without curiosity. The account code leads to a cost centre labelled only CEL, and Milo, who had assumed it was a department, now has a door he cannot unsee; Fen's contentment unsettles him because he envies it.

w5bd.title: Under Grief
w5bd.summary: Back at the partition Zara slides him a copy of the contract opened at the appendices and says only 'Read it under grief.' In the ink that shows only to the grieving, Milo learns that CEL stands for Chief Executive Lich, that the Lich is Edric Thane, once a clerk, and that every soul sent under is harvested to keep him continuing; his cheerful framework for the job collapses.

w5bd.title: Eleven Thousand Names
w5bd.summary: Milo goes to Prava for the name behind a closure number and discovers the private ledger she is not permitted to keep, eleven thousand souls she onboarded and remembers. Finding Halvard Bell's name in it, and dozens more whose files crossed his own desk, turns the harvest from a figure on a balance sheet into people Milo personally sent under.

w5bd.title: A Process Improvement Opportunity
w5bd.summary: Milo reaches for the instinct he has always had and drafts a memo to Management framing the leak as an inefficiency he could optimise, the kind of initiative that gets a soul noticed and promoted. Zara reads it over his shoulder and says nothing at all, and the silence makes him reread the memo as something Edric Thane might once have written.

w5bd.title: Draft Saved
w5bd.summary: For days the memo sits in his outbox while Milo keeps closing accounts and hitting quota, and every closure now has a name from Prava's ledger. He asks Zara outright what she wants from him; she tells him to come to the all-hands, and he realises their entire friendship has been a training plan, and that he does not mind as much as he should.

w5bd.title: Confetti That Dissolves
w5bd.summary: At the all-hands in the bedrock amphitheatre the quarter's single graduation is announced and the confetti vanishes before it lands, while Prava weeps silently in the back row. Milo tears up the memo, and Zara, still facing the stage, lays out her offer in five flat sentences: no rebellion, a work stoppage, a union of the dead, filed correctly. He says yes, and for the first time it is a choice.

w5bd.title: The Signature Sheet
w5bd.summary: Milo follows Zara through the departments as she collects signatures, one tired soul at a time, beginning with Retention, whose cheerful staff turn out to be the readiest to stop hoping on schedule. He learns that organising is mostly patience and correct forms, and the dead stop being alone one name at a time.

w5bd.title: Line by Line
w5bd.summary: Milo builds the reconciliation of every soul ever sent under, matching closure numbers to Prava's eleven thousand names and filling six centuries of gaps from Old Fen's archive; Fen helps simply because a drawer was asked for, and Prava lends the ledger she is not permitted to have. The first line Milo restores is Halvard Bell's, and his talent for the work finally points the right way.

w5bd.title: Filed Through Reconciliations
w5bd.summary: Zara and Milo submit the restructuring of Edric Thane's own pooled account through the department built to close accounts, every box correct, every appendix cited. Within the hour Milo receives a calendar invitation to his quarterly review in the corner office, and Zara, for the first time, looks up.

w5bd.title: Mr. Voss
w5bd.summary: Edric Thane receives Milo courteously, reviews his numbers, and offers him exactly what he once wanted: recognition, promotion, the path Edric himself climbed. Milo, recognising himself across the desk six centuries on, understands that saying yes would make him the next Edric, and declines.

w5bd.title: A Single Sheet of Paper
w5bd.summary: Milo hands over his resignation with the reconciliation attached, every soul's tenure restored and the pooled account zeroed by Edric's own rules, and says aloud what no one has: that Edric never took the onward because he is afraid of it. The Lich reads it the way a clerk reads, finds it correct, and the threat of restructuring Milo has nowhere left to land.

w5bd.title: Filed Correctly
w5bd.summary: Edric Thane, a clerk undone by a clerk, countersigns in the correct box, files the reconciliation himself, and goes onward. With the owner gone, the Pipeline must explain itself to its customers in plain language, and the work stoppage goes out as an all-staff email that is, for once, completely honest.

w5bd.title: Sometimes Quieter
w5bd.summary: Milo comes back down to Reconciliations and sits beside Zara, who does not look up, and this time he understands it as company rather than distance. His boredom returns, and he recognises it at last not as a personality but as the place his questions used to be.

In its place was a large, bright atrium with no windows. The light came evenly from everywhere and from nowhere in particular, the way it does in places built to keep people waiting. At the top of the chart, above all the boxes, two words were printed in a heavy serif: UNDEATH PIPELINE.

"Sorry, quick one," Milo said, tapping it. "Love the visual. But just so I've got the big picture before I dive into the details, what does the Pipeline actually, like, do? Deliverables-wise. What's the core output?"

"It's a wonderful question," Prava said. "Orientation covers all of that. You'll get a packet."

"Totally. And the packet, is it more of a high-level overview, or does it get into the actual mechanics? Because I always find I do my best work when I can see the whole flow, input to output."

"It's very thorough," Prava said. "Everyone says so. And honestly, Mr. Voss, the people who ask that question first tend to be exactly the people we want."

He opened his mouth to ask it a third way, and found that the question had gone soft at the edges, the way a dream does when someone speaks to you. It was still there. He could have picked it up again. It just did not seem to weigh as much as the other thing she had said, the thing underneath all the words: that someone had looked at forty-one years of him being bored, carefully and on purpose, and had written down valuable.

Prava drew a lanyard from a drawer, pale gray with a blank plastic sleeve, and laid it across the org chart.

"So what we'd be looking at," she said, "is a start on Monday, in Reconciliations, which is a team where we really feel your—"

"Yes," Milo said.

She paused, and he heard what he had done, and he did not take it back.

"Sorry. Yes. Sorry, I jumped in there, that's a me thing. But yes, absolutely, a hundred percent. Monday works. Monday is honestly ideal, because it gives me a clean runway, and I can hit the ground on day one instead of ramping into a short week, you know?"

Nobody had asked him a question. He noticed that a second too late, and then it did not seem important, because she was nodding, and the nod was for him.

He picked up the lanyard. It weighed almost nothing. He put it over his head and straightened it on his chest, and the plastic sleeve settled against his shirt with a small, satisfying click, like a part going into the place that had been machined for it.

Prava smiled at him. It was softer now, and very patient, and it stayed on him a little longer than the moment needed, the way you might look at a photograph you had already seen many times.

"Welcome aboard, Mr. Voss," she said.

He beamed back at her. He felt useful.

Reconciliations turned out to be a single room so long that its far end went faintly blue, like a road in summer. There were no windows. There were desks, in pairs, facing each other across low beige partitions, and at almost every desk someone was writing, and nobody was talking.

His desk was number forty-one. Milo chose to find that encouraging.

He set down the lanyard first, then picked it up again and put it back on, because a lanyard on a desk looked like someone who had stepped out. The in-tray was empty. He squared it to the corner of the blotter, adjusted it a quarter-inch, and then adjusted it back. He tested the chair's height lever. He tested the pen. The pen worked, which felt like a good sign about the organization as a whole.

Across the partition sat a woman with her head bent over a form. She had not looked up when he arrived. She did not look up when the chair squeaked, or when he cleared his throat at what he judged to be a friendly volume. Her pen moved in short, exact strokes and then stopped, and then moved again.

Milo knew that kind of stillness. It was the stillness of somebody very good at their job.

He very much wanted her to think the same of him.


He leaned over the partition, not too far, and put out his hand.

"Hi! Milo. Milo Voss. New hire, obviously, first day, so apologies in advance for all the dumb questions, but I figure better to front-load them now than circle back later and slow you down, right? Anyway. Really great to meet you. Really great to be here."

The pen stopped.

She looked up. Her eyes were grey, an even and unremarkable grey, like the side of a filing cabinet, and they rested on him for exactly one second. He could have counted it. Then they went back to the form.

"Zara Okafor."

That was all. She did not take the hand. After a moment Milo turned it into a sort of wave and then into a gesture at his own in-tray, as if that had been the plan.

He was not discouraged. If anything, he was impressed. Two words, full name, no filler. He had worked with people like that, the ones who had no time for small talk because they were carrying the whole department, and in his experience they were the best people to sit beside. You just had to earn it.

He sat back down, smiling. She had told him her name. That was a start.


He gave it almost a full minute.

"So, quick question on targets," he said. "Is there a number per day we're tracking against, or is it more of a weekly cadence? Because I can work either way, I just like to know which way the scoreboard faces."

"Your queue comes in the tray," Zara said. "Work the tray."

"Love that. Super clear. And when I finish the tray, is there like a shared pool I can pull from, so I'm not sitting idle? Because idle time is basically just a bottleneck wearing a nice shirt."

"You don't pull. You wait."

"Got it, got it. And the metrics, where do those live? Is there a board somewhere, or does someone send a summary at the end of the week, or—"

"Somebody else's numbers are somebody else's," Zara said. "Yours are what's in the tray."

Milo nodded slowly, the way he nodded in kickoff meetings when a framework was coming together. Work the tray. Don't pull. Ignore the board. It was minimalist, he decided. Almost elegant. Most places buried you in dashboards. This place had stripped everything back to one input and one output, and asked you to trust the process.

He took out a fresh sheet of paper and wrote, at the top, THE TRAY, and underlined it twice.


"Honestly, this is so refreshing," he said, mostly to the sheet of paper. "At my old place I spent a whole quarter getting our reporting cycle from nine days down to six. Nine to six! I remember the Friday we closed it out. Everybody went home on time. I sat in the parking lot for twenty minutes afterward just, you know, feeling it." He laughed a little at himself. "Probably the high point of my life, if I'm being real. Is that sad? That's sad, isn't it."

Zara turned a page.

"It won't be the high point here," she said. "Here you'll get a great many Fridays. You'll stop counting them before they stop coming."

Milo laughed, a real laugh, louder than the room was used to. Two desks down someone's pen paused and then went on. It was a good line. Dry, deadpan, exactly the kind of thing people said to each other once they had decided you were all right. He felt the warm little click of being let in on something.

"Oh, that's good," he said. "That's really good. I'm stealing that."

Across the partition Zara did not smile. She looked at him a moment longer than she had before, level and unblinking, the way someone looks at a line item before deciding which column it belongs in. Then she turned back to her screen.

Milo was still grinning at his underlined word.

"Milo?"

It was an org chart.

Some of the labels he couldn't quite follow. INTAKE he got. ORIENTATION, sure. RETENTION, RECORDS, RECONCILIATIONS, all in a neat row like siblings in a photograph. Above them a thick band marked MANAGEMENT, and above that one small box with three letters in it that he assumed was a subsidiary.

Prava folded her hands around her mug. It had no steam coming off it, and she did not drink from it.

"So here's the good news," she said. "You've been retained."

"Retained," Milo repeated.

"We looked at your file. Forty-one years in operations." She said the number the way other people said the names of countries they'd always wanted to visit. "Process improvement. Cycle times. You're a strong culture fit, Milo. A very strong one. We'd like you to start Monday, in Reconciliations."

She tapped the chart, the third box in the row, and left her finger there a moment so he could see it.

Milo looked at the box. Then he looked at her, and she was still smiling, and the smile had not moved at all while she said any of it.

Forty-one years. He had been good at them, every one. He had shaved days off workflows that made a component that went into a component that went into something nobody could name. He had been thanked for it twice, once by email. And here was a woman with a lanyard who had read the whole file, apparently, all the way to the bottom, and had come out the other end wanting more of it.

Something in his chest that he had assumed was gone sat up and paid attention.

"Now, if you'd like a moment to—" Prava began.

"Yes," Milo said. "Yes. Absolutely. Sorry, I don't mean to jump the queue, it's just, Monday works great for me, Monday is honestly ideal." He was leaning forward. He could feel himself leaning forward. "Is there a standard onboarding timeline? Like a thirty-sixty-ninety, or is it more of a learn-on-the-job situation? Either's fine. I'm genuinely flexible on ramp-up."

"We'll get you a mentor," said Prava. "And a desk. And a lanyard."

"Love that."

She turned a form around to face him. It was short, and most of it was already filled in, in a handwriting that was not his. There was a single box at the bottom marked INITIAL HERE. She offered him a pen. He took it.

M.V.

It was only as he lifted the nib from the paper that it occurred to him, in a mild, administrative way, that she had not finished her sentence. That nobody had asked him anything, actually. Not whether he wanted it. Not what Reconciliations reconciled.

The thought sat there for a second, small and cold, like a draft from a door someone had left open.

Milo decided it was nerves. Good nerves. First-day nerves.

He handed back the pen and smiled.

Monday came, though Milo could not have said how he knew. Nobody had a watch. The lanyard had arrived, though, clipped to his collar in the night like a tag on a coat, and it said VOSS, M. — RECONCILIATIONS, so that seemed to settle it.

A clerk with a clipboard walked him down a corridor and through a pair of doors and left him there without a word.

Reconciliations was a long room the colour of old teeth. The light came from nowhere in particular; it simply was, evenly, on everything, so that nothing in the room had a shadow worth mentioning. Desks ran in two rows down its length, each pair divided by a low partition, and at every desk someone was bent over a screen, and nobody looked up.

His desk was the fourth on the left. It had a chair, a monitor, an in-tray, and a drawer with a small brass lock. Across the partition sat a woman in a dark cardigan, typing.

Her nameplate said ZARA OKAFOR. She did not look up.

Milo sat down, adjusted his chair, adjusted it back, and arranged his face into the expression of a man who thought being ignored was a sign of a busy, high-performing team. He held it. It was fine. It was completely fine.


"Hi," he said, to the top of her head. "Milo. Voss. New. I think I'm the—I think you're my mentor? They said I'd get a mentor."

The typing stopped.

Zara Okafor raised her eyes. They were grey, flat as a filing cabinet, and they rested on him for exactly one second, long enough for Milo to feel weighed, measured and filed under a heading he could not read. Then they went back to the screen.

"Your queue is on the left," she said. "Work it top to bottom. Anything that isn't in it isn't yours."

That was all. The typing resumed.

Milo waited for the second half, the slide deck, the shared drive, the forty-minute walkthrough with a laminated quick-reference card. It didn't come. He found, a little to his surprise, that he didn't mind.

Two sentences. Scope, process, boundary. No preamble, no icebreaker, no asking him to share a fun fact about himself. He had sat through three-day onboardings that conveyed less. There was something almost beautiful about it, the way there was something beautiful about a spreadsheet with no merged cells.

He looked at the back of her monitor with a warmth he had not felt toward a colleague in years.

She was, he thought, a real operator.


Still, a real operator would want metrics. Milo rolled his chair an inch toward the partition, then another inch, until the casters bumped the base of it.

"Quick one," he said. "Totally no pressure. Is there a dashboard for the queue? Or, like, a team tracker, a shared sheet, anything where we're logging volume? Because I'm a big believer in visibility. If we can see the throughput, we can manage the throughput, right?"

Zara typed.

"Because, full transparency, that's kind of my wheelhouse. At my last place I built a tracker from scratch, pretty much on my own time, and it took eleven percent off our cycle time. Eleven. Which doesn't sound like a lot until you annualize it." He paused to let her annualize it. "So if there's a gap there, I'd love to own it."

Zara did not look up. "Read the appendices."

"The—sorry?"

"The contract has appendices. Read them. All of them, start to finish, before you close anything you can't take back."

"Love it," said Milo, and meant it. He pulled a notepad from the drawer and wrote, at the top of a fresh page, READ APPENDICES (ALL), and underlined it twice. Documentation-first. It was the kind of culture you could build something on.


He tapped the pen against the pad, still riding it. "Honestly? That tracker week? Best week of my life. Hands down. I know that sounds a little sad when you say it out loud."

"It's still the best one," Zara said. "Of your death as well. The rest just haven't happened to you yet."

Milo laughed. It came out of him easily, the big reflexive laugh he used to give in all-hands meetings when the VP made a joke about the coffee, and it went up into the light that came from nowhere and didn't come back down.

Zara did not laugh. She did not smile, either, or look up, or do the little exhale through the nose that people did to show they knew they'd been funny. She simply went on typing, at the same speed as before.

Down the row, nobody else had looked up.

Milo stopped laughing, slowly, the way a car rolls to a stop on a flat road.

Dry, he decided. Bone dry. The kind of person who delivered a line and let you find it yourself. He had worked with people like that before, and they were always, once you got past the first quarter, the best ones.

He rolled his chair back to his own side of the partition, feeling something warm settle in his chest.

He had a friend at work.

When he opened his eyes he was standing up, which seemed presumptuous of him.

The room was very large and very gray. It was the gray of a carpet sample, of a filing cabinet in a basement, of a sky that has decided not to commit to anything. There were no windows. Milo looked for a clock out of the same reflex that makes a person pat their pockets, and there was no clock, only a smooth gray wall where a clock would have gone if anyone had approved the requisition.

In his right hand was a paper ticket, the tear-off kind from a deli counter. It said 4,117.

He held it for a while. He waited to feel something large and appropriate, the way people in films felt things, and what arrived instead was a small, warm prickle at the back of his neck that he recognised at once. It was the feeling of walking into an orientation session ten minutes late, when everyone already has a name badge and a lanyard and a pastry, and the facilitator is on slide four.

"Sorry," Milo said quietly, to the room in general. "Sorry, is this the—sorry."

Nobody told him what it was the. He smoothed his tie, which was still there, and decided that was a good sign.

Above a row of counters at the far end of the atrium hung a red digital display. It read 3,902. Milo watched it in the patient, slightly narrowed way he had once watched a progress bar during a software migration, and it continued to read 3,902.

Between him and the counters stood the others. There were a great many of them, arranged in a line that folded back on itself through retractable belt barriers, the kind airports use, and every one of them held a ticket and looked at nothing. An old woman in a hospital gown. A man in cycling gear, still clipped into one shoe. A teenager holding his ticket the way people hold a phone. Nobody spoke. Nobody cried, either, which Milo noted, and filed, and did not examine.

He found that he was counting the counters. Six. Two staffed. He found that he was estimating average handle time. He found, with something close to relief, that he had opinions.

A second display, for one thing, showing the next five numbers, so people could plan. Separate lines for simple and complex cases. Seating. Honestly, at this volume, a kiosk.

"Okay," he murmured, to nobody, nodding. "Okay. Quick wins."

The display still said 3,902. He did not mind. Somewhere behind the quick wins there was a larger thought trying to get his attention, and he let the queue stand in front of it.

There was a soft electronic chime, the sound a lift makes when it has arrived somewhere it would rather not discuss, and the display went from 3,902 to 4,117 without passing through anything in between.

"Four thousand one hundred and seventeen," said a woman's voice from one of the staffed counters. It was a lovely voice. It was warm in the exact, rehearsed way of every reception desk he had ever approached with a lanyard question, a voice that had said the same number-shaped sentence so many times it had worn smooth. "Four one one seven, whenever you're ready, love."

Milo looked down at his ticket, then up at the display, then down again, the way one double-checks a boarding pass.

"That's me," he said, to the man in cycling gear, who did not respond. "Sorry, that's me, I think they've maybe got a priority track running, which, honestly, great call, love that."

He straightened his tie. He tucked the ticket into his breast pocket, then took it back out, in case they needed it, which they would, because there was always a form.

And there it was, rising through him as he walked toward the counter, a feeling so unfamiliar it took him three steps to name it. Not grief. Not fear. Something brisk and bright. There was a process here. Someone had built it. And he was going to be very, very good at it.

On the counter, beside a cup of pens and a small dish of individually wrapped mints, stood an engraved nameplate in brushed metal. PRAVA, it said. And underneath, smaller: INTAKE.

"Milo Voss," she said. "There you are. Welcome, Milo."

He had not said his name. He was fairly sure he had not said his name. He checked the ticket in his hand, which said only 4,117, and then he decided, with a little rush of approval, that this was what good pre-work looked like. Somebody had read the file before the meeting. Somebody had prepped.

"Hi! Wow. Okay, hi, yes, that's me," he said. "Sorry, I love that you already have my details, that's honestly a really seamless intake experience. Prava, is it? Great nameplate."

"Thank you, love," said Prava. "It was a gift."


She reached beneath the counter and brought up a sheet of card sealed in plastic, and slid it across to him with two fingers, the way a croupier slides chips. The laminate of the org chart whispered against the laminate of the desk. It was a very large chart. At the top was a single box with no name in it. Beneath that, boxes multiplied downward like a family tree that had lost interest in love and taken up logistics.

"Now, the good news," said Prava. "You've been retained."

"Retained," Milo repeated. "Okay. Great. Retained by—?"

"By us." She tapped a box near the bottom, where a line of small print said RECONCILIATIONS. "We've had a look at your background, and I'll be honest with you, love, it's a strong culture fit. Forty-one years in operations. Process work. Very steady. That's exactly what they want down there."

Nobody had ever called his background a fit for anything. People had called it fine. His last manager had called it reliable, in the tone used for dishwashers.

"You'll start Monday," Prava said. "Desk, lanyard, mentor. All arranged."

Milo looked at the little box marked RECONCILIATIONS as if it might, at any moment, wave. Something was happening in his chest, in the place where things used to happen. It felt, absurdly, like being picked first.


"Okay, so, a couple of quick questions, and stop me if these are covered in a deck somewhere," Milo said, leaning in until the bolted chair objected. "Is there a formal onboarding plan, like a thirty-sixty-ninety? And how do we measure success in Reconciliations, is it volume-based, or quality-based, or some kind of blended scorecard? Because I'm genuinely happy either way, I just like to know what good looks like before I start, so I'm not, you know, optimising for the wrong thing."

"There's a quota," said Prava. "You'll find it very manageable."

"Love a quota. Love that. Is it weekly or—"

"Quarterly." She turned a page of something under the counter. "They had a good look at your forty-one years, Milo. They've assessed all of it as an asset."

He opened his mouth to say thank you and what came out instead was, "Yes. Absolutely. Yes, count me in, a hundred percent, I'm in."

Prava smiled at him with great kindness.

He searched it carefully, the way he would search a contract for the signature line, and could not find, anywhere in it, the part where anyone had asked.


He decided it did not matter. Plenty of good things happened without anyone asking. Promotions, for instance. Weather.

"You'll do beautifully," Prava said, and she said it as if she had checked.

"Thank you! Honestly, thank you, that means a lot, and I just want to say this has been a really positive first touchpoint, like if there's a feedback survey I'm giving this a five." He was already half out of the bolted chair, scanning the far wall, where a row of illuminated signs hung over a row of identical doors. ORIENTATION. RECORDS. RETENTION. It was gray, with a plastic sleeve, and in the sleeve was a card that said VOSS, M. — RECONCILIATIONS — PROBATIONARY. He put it on at once and kept touching it on the walk down, the way a man touches a new wedding ring.

Reconciliations was a single long room that went on further than seemed structurally responsible. The ceiling hummed. The light came evenly from everywhere and nowhere, so that nobody cast a shadow, and the desks ran away in two straight lines toward a vanishing point that probably had a printer in it. The attendant who had walked him down stopped at an empty desk, gestured at it as one might gesture at a view, and left.

"Zara Okafor," she said. "I'm training you. Sit."

"Hi! Milo. Milo Voss. Wow, okay, a dedicated trainer, that's fantastic, honestly I didn't even know if there'd be a buddy system." He sat. The chair rolled an inch toward her, as if it too were keen. "Zara. Great. I'm really looking forward to working with you."

She typed a full line before she answered. "Good."


"Tenure," Zara said, to her screen. "You earn it by working. You spend it on leaving. That's all it's for."

"Okay, so it's kind of like a points system? Is it per task or per hour? And is there a dashboard where I can see my balance, or is it more of a quarterly statement situation?"

"Quarterly."

"Great. Love quarterly. Very digestible."

"Quota." Her fingers did not stop. "Accounts closed per quarter. Miss it, you go down the curve. Someone's always at the bottom."

"Right, a curve, totally, I've worked with curves. And are the quotas set top-down or is there a calibration conversation? Because sometimes when you're new there's a ramp period, and I'd love to understand whether—"

"Graduation," said Zara. "One per quarter. They announce it at the all-hands. There's confetti."

"Oh, that's nice. That's actually really nice. One per department, or—?"

"One."

He waited for the rest of the sentence. It did not come. The ceiling hummed. Down the long room, at desk after desk, other people typed and did not look up, and the sound of it was like rain on a roof that had never had a house beneath it.

"One total," Milo said. "Okay. Cool. Competitive." He nodded several times, to fill the space where she was not nodding back.


For a while nobody said anything. Milo logged in, which took four passwords and a security question about his first pet that he answered correctly and then felt oddly sad about. The typing went on around him, even and unhurried. Someone several desks down stamped something, once, and the stamp sounded like a dropped book in a library.

He leaned toward the partition and lowered his voice, the way you do in a lift.

"Can I ask a dumb question? And honestly, feel free to park it if it's out of scope. Is it always this quiet? Like, is this a heads-down culture, or is it just a Monday thing, or is there a social channel somewhere I haven't been added to yet?"

Zara considered her screen.

"No," she said. "Some days are quieter."

Milo laughed. It came out of him louder than he had meant, a real laugh, the kind he used to save for the one colleague per job who got it, and it went off down the long room and did not come back. Nobody looked up. Zara did not look up.

But she had made a joke. He was almost sure she had made a joke, and she had made it to him, on his first day, which in his experience was how the good working relationships started. He grinned at the side of her head and decided they were going to be friends.


He had turned back to his own screen, and was reading a welcome message that said WELCOME in four fonts, when Zara spoke again.

"At intake. You said yes fast. Why?"

It was the first thing she had asked him. Milo swivelled round, delighted, the way he used to swivel when a senior stakeholder finally put a question to the room.

"Oh! Great question. Honestly? I think it's because nobody's ever framed my experience as a value-add before, you know? Like, for forty-one years it was just, Milo does the spreadsheets, Milo fixes the handoffs, and that's fine, I genuinely enjoyed it, but nobody ever said strong fit, nobody ever said asset. And then she just said it, right out of the gate, and I guess I thought, okay, if someone's finally going to see the value, the least I can do is not make them wait for it. Does that make sense? That probably sounds a bit much."

Zara listened to all of it with her eyes on the screen. When he stopped she reached for a small pad by her keyboard and made a mark on it. A short one. Not a word, he thought. A tick, maybe, or the start of a tally.

"Okay," she said.

Milo turned back to the four fonts. He felt warm, and seen, and very faintly as if he had just been weighed.


Some time later, though there was no way to measure how much, Zara stood up. Milo stood up too, because she had, and followed her down the aisle to an alcove where a steel machine sat on a counter beside a stack of mugs.

The machine had one button. Zara pressed it. It thought about the request, made a noise like a long sigh through a drainpipe, and released a thin stream of something gray into her cup. Not coffee-gray. A grayer gray. The gray of a thing that remembered being coffee and had made its peace with no longer being so.

"Your first account's in your queue," she said, watching the cup fill.

"Oh, amazing. Already? Love a fast start."

He took a mug from the stack. It was white, chipped at the handle, and printed on the side in cheerful red letters it said THANK GOD IT'S FRIDAY. He looked at it for a moment, trying to recall when he had last seen a Friday, and then pressed the button.

The gray came out. He drank it. It tasted of very little, warmly. He drank it the way he had drunk ten thousand cups at ten thousand desks, without deciding to, his hand doing the thing it had always done, and it did not occur to him to ask why he was holding it at all.


Back at the desks, Zara rolled her chair to the end of the partition, close enough to see his screen. It was the nearest she had come.

"Open it."

He opened it. A single account filled the window: a reference number, a department code, a column of figures running down the right-hand side in a typeface designed for people who did not want to be interrupted. At the top, in a smaller font, there was a name. He read past it to the numbers, because the numbers were where the work was.

"Remaining tenure. Bottom of the column."

"Okay, got it. Wow, that's a lot of decimal places."

"Zero it."

He typed a zero into the field and pressed enter. The column recalculated itself from the bottom up, each line folding neatly into the next, until every figure read the same. It was, he thought, genuinely beautiful. It balanced. Nothing hanging, nothing pending, no open loop.

"Initial the box."

There was a box marked INITIAL HERE. He initialled it. M.V., in the little cursive flourish he had been using on expense reports since he was twenty-six.

"That's so clean," Milo said, and he meant it. "Honestly, the UX on this is so much better than our old system."

Somewhere above the numbers, the name sat where he had left it, unread.


He scrolled. There was one field left, at the very bottom of the form, below a thin double rule. It was labelled DISPOSITION, and it had already been filled in, not typed but printed into the template itself, in capitals, so that no one could ever enter anything else.

UNDER.

"Okay, so this last bit," Milo said, tapping the screen with the rim of his mug. "Under. Where is that, exactly? And I don't mean that in a weird way, I'm just a big believer in understanding the end-to-end, because if I know what happens downstream I can usually find efficiencies upstream, and honestly that's where I add the most value. Is it another department? A partner org? Is there a handoff doc?"

Zara looked at the word. She looked at it for longer than she had looked at him all day.

"It's not on the form," she said.

"Right, no, totally, but like, in general—"

"It's not on the form."

She said it exactly the same way the second time, with no more weight and no less, the way you might read a serial number back to someone who had misheard it. The ceiling hummed. Somewhere down the long room a stamp came down, once. Milo noticed that his mug had gone cold in his hand, and that he could not remember whether it had ever been warm.


He looked at the box again. UNDER. Five letters, capitalised, printed into the template so firmly it was practically load-bearing.

And he thought, well. Not every stakeholder needed visibility into every step. That was just true. He had said it himself, in meetings, to people who wanted to be copied on everything. You owned your piece. You trusted the process to own the rest. If there had been a reason for him to know where under was, someone would have put it on the form, and they had not, and that was, in its own way, a kind of answer.

The thought arrived whole and comfortable, like a chair that had been waiting for him. It was so easy. It was, he realised with a small private glow, the first thing in this place that he was genuinely good at.

"Okay," Milo said. "Makes sense. Filing it."

He clicked FILE. The account folded itself away with a soft chime, and the queue offered him the next one, already open, already waiting.

Beside him the typing had stopped. He registered it the way you register a fridge switching off, only by the quiet it left. He glanced across. Zara's hands were resting on her keyboard and her eyes were on his screen, not hers.

"All good?" he asked.

She began typing again.

The conference room had no windows, which Milo had always considered a feature. Windows invited comparison. On the screen a slide titled Q3 COMPONENT ALIGNMENT showed a box with an arrow pointing to a slightly larger box, and the slightly larger box had an arrow pointing off the edge of the slide, toward whatever it was all for. Nobody had ever scrolled far enough to find out.

It was a Tuesday. The projector hummed. Someone at the far end was saying "dependencies" in the patient voice of a man who expected to say it again.

Milo leaned toward the colleague beside him and lowered his voice.

"Not to be that guy, and I really do think there's value in getting everyone in the room, I'm a big believer in face time, genuinely, but if we're being honest with ourselves about the deliverable here, and I think we owe it to the stakeholders to be honest, this is kind of one of those meetings that, you know, could have—"

The colleague nodded without turning. Milo sat back, warmed. There was comfort in being bored where you were meant to be: on the clock, with a calendar invite to prove it.

He felt, on reflection, that the point deserved landing. He leaned in again.

"—could have been," Milo said, and then he did not say anything else.

It was not dramatic. There was no pain to speak of, only a sense of a tab closing somewhere. His chin was resting on his chest at an angle he would never have chosen in a meeting with leadership present, and he found that he was looking at it from slightly above and to the left.

The slide advanced. Q3 COMPONENT ALIGNMENT, CONTINUED.

The colleague beside him glanced over, then glanced at the clock on the wall, then raised a hand halfway.

"I think Milo's, ah," she said.

The man at the far end paused on "dependencies" and looked down the table with the expression of someone recalculating a timeline. "Okay," he said. "Let's take that offline."

Someone made a note. Someone else reached across and, very considerately, muted the laptop in front of Milo's body so its notifications would not interrupt. The meeting moved on to item four.

Milo understood. He had run meetings. You could not stop for everything. Still, he thought, from his new vantage near the ceiling tiles, it would have been nice to be an agenda item, even a short one, even one marked FYI.

The ceiling tiles went first, and then the idea of a ceiling. The room thinned out around him like a spreadsheet when someone hides the gridlines, and then there was no room, only gray. It was not dark and it was not light. It had no walls to lean on and no clock to watch, which he found harder to adjust to than the dying.

With nothing else on his calendar, Milo did what he always did with downtime. He ran a retrospective.

Forty-one years. He went through them the way he would go through a quarterly report, looking for the headline number. There was the tracker that had cut cycle time by eleven percent. There was the onboarding deck he had rebuilt twice. There was the approval workflow he had reduced from seven signatures to four, which had been, at the time, a genuine win for cross-functional alignment.

"Okay," he said to the gray, because it helped to say things out loud. "So what did the component actually do?"

The gray did not know. Neither, he realised, did he. He had made a great many things faster, and he could not name one of them that had needed to go anywhere.

He waited to feel bad about this. He felt, mostly, mildly curious, and then, more mildly, not even that.

Time passed, or something shaped like it. Milo could not have said how much. There was no clock, and without a clock he found he had no way to tell whether he was early.

That was the thing that began to bother him, eventually. Not the dying. Not the component. The not knowing what came next on the agenda.

"Hello?" he tried. "Just checking in. No rush on my end, I know everyone's slammed, I only wanted to flag that I'm sort of, I guess, available? If there's a next step, or an owner for this, or even just a point of contact, I'm happy to sync whenever works."

The gray took this under advisement.

He had been waiting, he realised, his whole life, for someone to tell him what the next action item was. He had simply never noticed, because someone always had. A manager, a calendar, a ticket in a queue. There had always been a box marked INITIAL HERE, somewhere, with his name already typed beneath it.

There would be one here too. There was always one. Somebody had to process him.

Milo sat up straighter, though there was nothing to sit on. His hand went to his collar and straightened a tie he was no longer wearing. He arranged his face into the expression he used on first days: open, eager, easy to work with.

Then he waited to be found.
rows.later:
He was found.

There was no transition to speak of. One moment there was gray, and the next there was a chair beneath him, molded plastic, the kind every waiting room had agreed on, and Milo opened his eyes in a hall so large it seemed to have been designed to make the people in it feel like rounding errors. The light came from everywhere and nowhere, soft and even, the color of a screen left on overnight. Somewhere a long way off, a printer was printing.

In front of him was a desk. It was laminate, faux walnut, with a small cactus on one corner that he suspected was also laminate. A nameplate faced him. PRAVA, it said. INTAKE.

Behind it sat a woman with tidy hair and a cardigan the color of weak tea, and she was already smiling at him, as though he were exactly on time.

"Milo," she said. "There you are. Welcome. Take a moment."

Her voice was warm in the way a hand is warm on a cold morning. Milo felt his shoulders come down from somewhere near his ears.

"Hi! Wow. Hi. Thank you, that's, yes, I'll take the moment, absolutely."

Someone had come for him. Someone had his file. It did not occur to him to wonder what was in it.


Prava opened a drawer, took out a sheet of laminated card and slid it across the desk with two fingers, the way one might offer a menu at a restaurant one was proud of.

It was an org chart. Milo knew org charts. This one was enormous, a great branching thing in small gray type, boxes upon boxes, with a single box at the very top that had been printed slightly smaller than the rest, as if out of modesty.

"You've been retained," Prava said.

"Retained," Milo repeated. "Like, as in—"

"We've reviewed your file. Forty-one years in process improvement. Cycle times. Workflows. Approvals." She said each word gently, the way one reads out the names of grandchildren. "You never once asked what any of it was for. That's rare, Milo. That's a strong culture fit."

Milo opened his mouth and found nothing in it.

No one had ever said that to him. Not his managers, who had said good job, and not his parents, who had said that's nice, dear, and certainly not himself. He had always assumed the boredom was a sort of weather he lived in. It had not occurred to him that it might be a skill.

"Wow," he said. "Okay. Wow. That's really, honestly, that's really validating to hear."

The atrium seemed to tilt, very slightly, toward him.


Prava touched one box on the chart with a fingernail. It was about two thirds of the way down, off to one side, connected to the rest by a single thin line.

"Reconciliations," she said. "You'll start Monday."

"Yes," Milo said. "Yes, absolutely, a hundred percent. Monday works great for me, I mean obviously my calendar has, ha, opened up quite a bit, but even if it hadn't, I'd move things, I'm very much a whatever-the-team-needs person. And Reconciliations, that's, so that's accounts? Closing things out? Because I love closing things out. Honestly, a clean close is maybe my favorite part of any quarter. So yes. Count me in. Thank you. Really."

He stopped to breathe, out of habit, and found he did not need to.

Prava was nodding, warmly, as though he had said something sensible.

It was only then, looking down at the laminated card, that Milo noticed her finger had never moved. It was still resting on the one box. There had been no other box. There had been, now that he replayed it, no question either. She had not said would you like, or how do you feel about. She had said you'll start.

He had said yes to a sentence that had not needed one.

That was fine, he decided. That was efficient.


Prava drew a manila folder from beneath the org chart. His name was already typed on the tab, VOSS, MILO, in a font he recognised from every form he had ever been handed. She opened it, made a small mark, and brought down a rubber stamp with a soft, final thud.

RETAINED, it said, upside down.

"Welcome aboard," she said. "I hope you'll be very happy with us."

She smiled at him, and the smile stayed. It stayed past the point where a smile has finished saying what it came to say, past the point where Milo would have looked down at his notes, if he had had notes. Her eyes were kind and wet at the edges, the way eyes get from long hours under bright light.

"Me too," Milo said. "I mean, I will be. I'm sure. Thank you, Prava."

He had read it off the nameplate. That was how he knew her name.

She had not read his off anything. She had said it the moment he opened his eyes, before the folder came out, before he had said a single word.

Milo noticed this. He held it up to the soft, sourceless light for a second, the way he might hold up a receipt that did not quite add up.

Then he put it in a drawer at the back of his mind, and smiled back, and let her be kind to him.


Orientation was held in a beige room with beige chairs and a carpet that had been chosen, Milo suspected, specifically so that no one would ever remember it. There were eleven other new hires. None of them spoke. They had the startled, well-behaved look of people who had recently stopped mid-sentence.

The facilitator moved down the row with a box of lanyards, hanging one around each neck with the brisk tenderness of a nurse. Milo's said VOSS, M. — RECONCILIATIONS — PROVISIONAL. He touched it. It felt like belonging.

"Glossary," the facilitator said, and the lights dimmed.

RESTRUCTURED, said the first slide. When a soul's contract is updated to reflect its transition under.

UNDER, said the next. The destination of a restructured soul, as authorised by the CEL.

THE CEL, said the third. The authorising function for all restructurings.

"Any questions?" the facilitator asked, in the voice of someone who had asked it many times and been answered never.

Milo wrote it all down. He underlined UNDER twice and drew a small box around THE CEL. It felt good. It felt like the first week of any job, the comforting rain of acronyms, the sense that a great deal was being handled by someone, somewhere, competently.

He did not raise his hand. Everything, he felt, had been very clearly covered.


Still, it was good practice to map the stakeholders. Milo took out the laminated org chart, which he had been allowed to keep, and laid it across his knees.

He found Reconciliations easily enough, two thirds down and off to the side. He found Intake, and Records, and Retention, and a long horizontal band labelled MANAGEMENT that seemed to have more boxes than people could possibly fill. He did not find the CEL. He looked twice. The only box it could be was the small one at the very top, the modest one, and that box had no name in it at all. Just three letters, in the same gray type as everything else.

Well. That settled it. People did not get three-letter boxes. Functions did.

Milo had survived four reorganisations in life and recognised the type. A shared-services thing, probably. Corporate Enterprise Logistics. Central Executive Liaison. One of those departments that nobody could explain and everyone had to route through, and that sent out quarterly memos about process alignment that no one finished reading.

He wrote, in the margin of his notes, CEL = dept. (Corp. Ent. Logistics?), and felt the small, clean pleasure of a box ticked.

"Makes sense," he said, half to himself.

Around him, eleven lanyards nodded, or did not. The facilitator, clicking to the next slide, said nothing at all.


Afterwards a clerk collected him at the door. The clerk had a clipboard, a lanyard of his own, and the gait of a man who had walked the same route so many times the route had started walking him.

"This way," the clerk said.

The corridors of the Marrow District were gray in a way Milo had not known gray could be: gray floors, gray walls, gray ceilings, gray light humming down from long tubes, and not a single window, as though windows had been considered and found to be a distraction. There were no clocks either. He kept glancing for one out of habit.

"So, quick question," Milo said, hurrying to keep up, "is there a standard intake-to-close workflow for Reconciliations, or is it more of a case-by-case, own-your-queue kind of situation? Because I'm comfortable either way, I've worked in both environments, I just like to know going in."

"Left," said the clerk.

They passed a coffee station dispensing something gray into a paper cup that nobody was holding. They passed a corkboard. Pinned to it was a newsletter, THE PIPELINE, with a cartoon of a smiling soul giving a thumbs up and a headline about quarterly morale.

"Oh, fun, a newsletter! Is there a submissions process, or—"

"Right," said the clerk.

Milo's voice went on ahead of them down the corridor and came back to him, a little thinner, unanswered.


The last door said RECONCILIATIONS in small, apologetic capitals. The clerk opened it, pointed at a desk, and was gone before Milo could thank him.

It was a long room, longer than it needed to be, lined with low partitions and lit from nowhere in particular. Rows of the dead sat at rows of desks, closing things. Pens moved. Paper turned. Someone stamped something with great care. The quiet had a texture, like felt.

Milo set his lanyard straight, put his folder down on the empty desk, and turned to face the room the way he had faced every room on every first day.

"Hi, everyone! I'm Milo, I'm new, obviously, ha. Reconciliations, starting today, well, Monday technically, but I figured, why not get a jump on things. Anyway, if anybody needs a hand with anything, literally anything, overflow, filing, a second pair of eyes, I'm right here. Happy to help."

Nobody looked up.

It was not rude. That was the strange part. No one sighed, no one shushed him. A few heads gave the smallest tilt, the way one acknowledges weather. Then the pens went on moving.

Milo sat down. The chair made no sound. He folded his hands on the desk and smiled at the partition in front of him, and the partition, politely, did not smile back.


There was someone at the next desk. Milo had not noticed her at first, which he would later think said something about her, or about him. She sat a foot away across the low partition, writing in small, square letters on a form he could not read upside down. Her sleeves were rolled to the elbow. Her hair was pinned back with what looked like a bent paperclip.

Milo rolled his chair an inch toward the partition, then another inch, and leaned his forearms on the top of it.

"Hi! Sorry, I don't want to interrupt your flow, I know how it is when you're heads-down, but I figured since we're going to be neighbours, desk-wise, I should probably just, you know, say hello properly. I'm Milo. Voss. Milo Voss. New. Ops background, mostly process, some light change management, a little bit of everything really. Very excited to be here. Very much looking forward to learning the ropes."

The pen did not stop.

"Zara Okafor," she said. "Your trainer."

She did not look up. She did not put the pen down. She turned the form over and began on the back.

Milo sat back, delighted. Two words, then two more. No small talk, no fuss. He had worked with people like this before, people who respected your time. It was, he decided, a kind of welcome.


"Great. Great! So, Zara, while I've got you, and stop me if this is a later conversation, but in terms of volume, roughly what kind of throughput are we looking at per analyst, per week? Ballpark is fine. I just like to have a number in my head so I know if I'm tracking."

"Depends."

"Totally, totally, it always does. And are there documented best practices anywhere, like a runbook, or is it more tribal knowledge at this point? Because if it's tribal knowledge, no judgment, I've actually got some experience capturing that kind of thing into templates."

"Ask me."

Milo nodded. Ask me. That was practically an open door.

"Love that. Okay, and then last one, I promise, ish. What does a really strong first quarter look like for someone in my seat? What would make you go, wow, that new guy's actually adding value?"

The pen paused at the end of a line, crossed a t, moved on.

"Close your queue."

"Close my queue," Milo repeated, and wrote it on the inside of his folder, and underlined it.

Each answer was short, but each answer was an answer. That was more than the clerk had given him, and more than orientation had given him, and a good deal more, frankly, than the gray. He felt a small warmth gathering, like the first hours of a team-building retreat that might actually turn out to be fun.


He let a little silence go by, to show he could. It was harder than he expected. The room had a way of filling any pause with its own pause: the soft scratch of pens, a stamp coming down three desks away, a sheet of paper being turned over by someone who seemed to have all of eternity to turn it.

Milo leaned in again, lowering his voice to match.

"Can I ask, and this is a genuinely curious question, not a complaint, I'm actually a big fan of a focused environment, but is it always this quiet in here? Or is it, like, a Monday thing? Or I guess a pre-Monday thing, technically."

"Sometimes it's quieter."

Milo laughed. It came out louder than he meant it to, and two heads down the row tilted, very slightly, and tilted back.

"Ha! Okay. Okay, that's good. Sometimes it's quieter. I like that."

He sat back, grinning at the partition. There it was. A bit. Everyone had a bit, and once you knew someone's bit you were halfway to lunch together, and halfway to lunch was most of the way to a friend. He could already picture it: the two of them by the coffee station, him doing the talking, her doing the dry little lines.

Across the partition, the pen kept moving. Her face did not change at all.


Milo turned back to his own desk, pleased with the morning. It was an empty desk, which was fine; empty desks were potential. There was a blotter, a pen in a holder, a tray marked IN and a tray marked OUT, and a third tray, unlabelled, that he decided not to have an opinion about yet. He squared the folder against the edge of the blotter. He moved the pen half an inch to the left, then back.

"Okay," he said, mostly to himself. "Okay. Let's do this."

At the edge of his vision, something across the partition changed.

The scratching had stopped. Zara's pen was resting on the desk, uncapped. Her hand had gone to a notebook he had not seen before, a narrow black one with a worn spine, lying under the forms, and she turned a single page of it, and then another, the way one turns to the right section of a binder.

She did not write anything that he could see. She only looked at the page, then at the forms, then, for no longer than a breath, at the side of his desk.

Milo smiled. A separate notebook for the separate tasks. Colour-coded, probably, in private. He liked her more for it.

Organised, he thought, approvingly, and straightened his lanyard, and waited for his queue.

It was a Tuesday, which Milo would later feel was the least he deserved.

The meeting was in Conference Room C, the one with the projector that hummed in B-flat, and it had been going for fifty-one minutes, and in that time it had produced one action item, which was to schedule a follow-up meeting.

Milo leaned toward the colleague beside him and lowered his voice to the register reserved for honesty.

"I'm not saying it's nobody's fault, and I'm definitely not saying it's anybody's fault, but if we're being really candid about value delivered versus time invested, this whole thing could honestly have been an email, or even, and I'm just floating this, a short bulleted—"

The sentence stopped.

It did not trail off. It did not break. It simply ended, the way a hallway ends at a wall, and Milo stood at the end of it with the next word still in his mouth.

He was mostly annoyed. He had been building to the bullets.

"—list," said Milo, to no one.

He was lying on his back. Above him, a long way above him, fluorescent tubes ran in parallel rows toward a vanishing point, each one buzzing at a slightly different pitch, none of them in B-flat. He sat up.

The room was gray. Not a decorative gray, not a slate or a dove or a heather, but the gray of a thing that had never been asked what color it wanted to be. It went on in every direction. There were no windows. He checked the walls twice, the way you check your pockets for keys, and there were no clocks either.

He patted himself down. No phone. No lanyard. No laptop, no pen, no coffee, not even the agenda he had been holding, which he had printed double-sided as a small act of protest.

All he had, as far as he could tell, was the rest of the sentence. He turned it over. It was still there, a short bulleted list, waiting for someone to agree with it.

A short way off stood a ticket dispenser on a chrome pole, the kind delicatessens use. As Milo approached, it extruded a paper tongue without being asked. He tore it off. It said 4,118,203.

Above the far wall a red display read NOW SERVING 4,117,960.

Milo did the subtraction automatically. Two hundred and forty-three ahead of him. He watched the display. It clicked over once, then again, and he counted between the clicks the way other people might count between lightning and thunder. Roughly nine seconds a soul. Call it thirty-six minutes, assuming steady state.

The queue itself was a marvel. Retractable belt barriers folded the waiting dead into a switchback so tight it could have been drawn with a ruler. Laminated signs said PLEASE HAVE YOUR DEATH READY and STAND BEHIND THE LINE UNTIL CALLED. Nobody was crying. Nobody was even talking.

Somewhere, Milo thought, a person had designed this, and that person had really understood flow.

He felt he ought to be panicking. He checked for it, the way he had checked for clocks. It was not there either.

At the end of the switchback sat an attendant at a podium, stamping something. Milo stepped up and waited to be noticed. He was not.

"Hi! Sorry. Quick one."

"You're deceased," the attendant said, without looking up. "Wait to be called."

"Right, no, totally, I got that, I think, broadly." Milo held up his ticket as a kind of credential. "I just wanted to get a sense of the overall framework here, like what the stages are, roughly, and who owns each handoff, because I'm someone who does better with a bit of visibility into the bigger picture, and also is there an SLA, or is it more best-effort?"

The attendant reached under the podium and slid a laminated card across it. FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS, it said. Every question on it was a variation of the word why. Every answer was PLEASE WAIT TO BE CALLED.

Milo read it twice. He found he was smiling.

He had been dead for perhaps ten minutes, and already there was a card for it.

The red display clicked. 4,118,203.

It was thirty-one minutes, not thirty-six. Milo noted the variance with approval and stepped out of the switchback, and a light came on above a row of desks on the far side of the atrium, as if the room had been expecting him particularly.

He walked toward it. His shoes made no sound on the gray floor, which he decided was a carpet decision rather than a metaphysical one.

Halfway there, he remembered the sentence.

He had never finished it. Somewhere behind him, in Conference Room C, a short bulleted list had been left hanging in the air, and nobody had agreed with it, and nobody ever would. He waited to mind.

Around him the dead shuffled forward with their tickets. No one looked back. No one seemed to be carrying anything unfinished, or if they were, they had folded it up small.

The pang came and went. Milo filed it, provisionally, under relief.

"Next," said someone at the desk, warmly.
