The desk was laminate, the chair was laminate, and the woman behind them had arranged herself so that both seemed to have been chosen for him. A small nameplate faced outward. PRAVA, it said, in a font that wanted to be friendly and had been told to be legible instead.

Milo sat. He put his ticket on the desk, squared it against the edge, and then, because that seemed insufficient, gave it a little pat.

"Milo Voss," Prava said, before he could open his mouth. She said it gently, the way you would say the name of a street you had grown up on. "Welcome. Take your time. There's no hurry here, Milo."

"Oh! Hi. Wow. Okay, so you already have my details, which is great, that's honestly a really strong first touchpoint, because in my experience the number one friction point in any intake flow is making people repeat information the system already holds, so kudos, genuinely, to whoever owns that piece."

Prava smiled. It was a good smile. It had the finish of something used often and kept clean.

Milo felt the warmth land on him like a lanyard. Somebody had prepared for him. Somebody had read his file. In forty-one years, he could not remember a meeting where that had been true.

This, he thought, was a well-run organisation.


Prava slid a laminated sheet across the desk. It was an org chart, dense with boxes, the lines between them so many and so fine that the whole thing looked less like a company than a root system.

"Aeon Holdings," she said. "You've been retained."

"Retained," Milo repeated. "Like, as in—"

"As in we'd like to keep you." She turned a page in his file. It was a thick file. He had not known he had a file. "Forty-one years in operations. Never missed a deadline. Never escalated. Never asked why a process existed, only how to make it faster." She looked up, and her eyes were kind. "That's rarer than you'd think, Milo. Most people waste a great deal of energy wondering."

"I mean, I always just figured the why was above my pay grade, and honestly there's a real efficiency in staying in your lane, so—"

"Exactly. You're a strong culture fit."

Milo sat with that. Nobody had ever called it a fit before. His mother had called it a phase. His manager had called it reliable, in the tone people use for dishwashers.

He had always thought of the boredom as something he had. It had never occurred to him it might be something he was good at.


Prava tapped a box near the middle of the chart. It was no bigger than the others, but more lines ran into it.

"You'll be starting Monday," she said. "In Reconciliations."

"Yes," said Milo. "Yes, absolutely, a hundred percent yes. And I want to say, just for the record, that I'm really flexible on start dates, so if Monday's tight on your end we can totally flex, and I'm happy to do any pre-reading, or shadowing, or whatever the ramp-up looks like, and if there's a buddy system I would love to be buddied, I'm extremely buddyable. Reconciliations! That's great. I love reconciling. I mean I've never formally reconciled, but conceptually? Huge fan."

He stopped, slightly out of breath, which was strange, since he was fairly sure he no longer needed it.

Prava was writing something in his file. She had not looked up during any of it. She did not seem to need to.

Milo replayed the last minute, the way he replayed meetings in the car. She had said Monday. She had said Reconciliations. He searched for the part where she had asked him whether he wanted it.

There was not one. There had not been a question at all. He had simply answered it, very thoroughly, in advance.


The stamp came down once, cleanly. RETAINED, it said, in red, slightly crooked, as if even the stamp had been doing this a long time.

Prava reached into a drawer and brought out a lanyard. It was gray, with a plastic sleeve at the end, and in the sleeve was a card bearing his name, his photograph, and a barcode. The photograph was from his driver's license. He had blinked in it. He had always hated it, and now it was going to last forever.

"Thank you," Milo said, and put it on. It weighed almost nothing. "Seriously. This has been, honestly, one of the best onboarding experiences I've ever had, and I've been onboarded a lot, so that's not nothing."

"It's not nothing," Prava agreed.

He stood. The chair slid back without a sound.

"Milo Voss," she said.

He turned. She was looking at him properly now, and she said it slowly, each syllable placed, the way you might set a cup on a high shelf where it would not get knocked.

"Yes?"

"Nothing," said Prava. "Just Milo Voss."

He smiled at her, warmed right through. She remembered him already. He had only been here half an hour, and somebody already knew his name.


Orientation was a room with forty chairs and one facilitator, and Milo was the only soul in it.

The facilitator was a narrow man with a clip-on tie who moved as if he were saving himself for something. He reached for Milo's lanyard without asking, threaded a second card onto it, and let it drop. RECONCILIATIONS, it said, in white on gray.

"Vocabulary," the facilitator said, and handed him a sheet.

It was two columns. On the left, under DO NOT SAY, were words like died and gone and taken. On the right, under PREFERRED, were words like transitioned, retained, restructured, sent under, graduated. At the bottom, in italics: Accurate language is the foundation of a respectful workplace.

"Oh, this is great," Milo said. "This is so great. Is there a laminated version? Not that this isn't great, it's just that I learn better when there's a physical artefact I can keep at my desk and kind of internalise over time, and also I want to make sure I'm using these in the right contexts, because I'd hate to say restructured when I mean retained, you know?"

"You won't," said the facilitator.

Milo read the right-hand column four times. By the fourth, it was his. Everything on it sounded handled.


The facilitator projected an org chart onto the wall. It was the same root system Prava had shown him, drawn larger, and this time Milo followed the lines properly.

Intake at the bottom, wide as a foundation. Orientation above it, then Assignment. Then the departments fanned out: Records, Retention, Reconciliations, and a dozen others he did not recognise, each with a column of smaller boxes underneath. Above them was a thick band labelled MANAGEMENT. Above Management, alone, a single box. Inside it were three letters: CEL.

Milo tilted his head. Corporate Enterprise something. Central Escrow and Ledgers, maybe. Some kind of holding entity, he guessed, the parent company's parent company, the sort of thing that existed mostly on letterhead and in the footer of quarterly reports.

"And CEL is the, what, the group-level entity?" he asked. "Like a holdco? Or is it more of a shared-services function?"

The facilitator looked at the box for a moment, then at Milo.

"It's at the top," he said, and advanced to the next slide.

Milo nodded, satisfied. He had not been corrected. In his experience, that meant he had got it right. He had read the whole structure in under a minute, which, for a first day, felt like a strong start.


The facilitator walked him there himself, which Milo took as a courtesy, though the man did not speak once on the way.

The Marrow District went on for a long time. Corridors opened onto open-plan floors that opened onto further corridors, all under the same flat fluorescent light, all at the same temperature, which was none. There were no windows anywhere. After the fifth floor Milo stopped looking for them, the way you stop listening for a fridge. Every so often they passed a coffee station, and at every coffee station someone was standing very still, holding a cup.

Reconciliations was a long, low room of partitioned desks. The facilitator stopped at an empty one, nodded at the chair, and left.

The desk faced a gray partition about chest height. On the far side of it a woman sat working, her eyes on her screen, her pen moving in small exact strokes. She did not look up. A nameplate on her side of the partition said ZARA OKAFOR.

Milo sat down very carefully, so as not to disturb her, and then sat there feeling it: a desk, a chair, and across from him another person, close enough to talk to. In forty-one years he had mostly had a wall.


He gave it a minute, to be polite. Then he leaned toward the partition.

"Hi! Sorry, I don't want to break your flow, I know how it is when you're heads-down, but I'm Milo, Milo Voss, I'm new, obviously, and I just wanted to put a face to the desk, so to speak, and say that I'm really excited to be on the team, and if there's anything I can take off your plate, even small stuff, honestly especially small stuff, just say the word."

The pen kept moving.

"Zara," she said. "Your queue loads at nine. Initial in the box. Don't use the stapler. It's mine."

"Totally. Great. Love that. Nine, initial, stapler." He nodded several times. "Clear ownership. That's so refreshing."

She turned a page. She did not look up.

Milo sat back. Five sentences, he counted, maybe six, and every one of them useful. Nobody at his old job had ever told him anything that useful in a whole week. People who did not like you did not tell you where the stapler stood. That was just how it worked.

The light hummed. The partition was gray. On his screen, a small icon spun, preparing his queue.

He had a neighbour, and a queue, and a box to initial. He waited for nine.

"—which honestly could have been an email," Milo said, and opened his eyes.

There was no meeting. There was no conference room, no lukewarm carafe, no Gary from Procurement sharing his screen. There was a desk, laminate, the colour of weak tea, and Milo was sitting at it with his hands folded on top as though he had been waiting a while and was being very patient about it.

The room was large and gray and had no windows. It didn't seem to have walls either, exactly. It went on in every direction the way a parking structure goes on, lit evenly from nowhere, and somewhere far off a printer was printing something long.

Milo checked his pockets. No phone. No badge. No pen, which was the one that worried him.

He straightened his tie, which he was also, he noticed, no longer wearing. He sat up anyway. He arranged his face into the expression he used for the first five minutes of any call with a new vendor: engaged, open, ready to align. It was a good face. It had got him through forty-one years of Tuesdays.

Whatever this was, he told himself, it was probably just onboarding.


Someone was sitting across the desk from him. He was fairly sure she had not been there a moment ago, and fairly sure it would be rude to mention it.

She was a small woman in a cardigan the colour of the room, with her hair pinned up the way people pin it when they have a long day ahead and have made their peace with it. A lanyard hung at her collar. The card on it said PRAVA in plain capitals, and underneath, smaller, INTAKE.

"Milo," she said, as if they had met before and she had been glad of it. "There you are. Take all the time you need."

Her voice was low and unhurried, the voice of someone who had said these exact words many times and meant them every time. Milo felt his shoulders come down an inch.

"Thanks so much," he said. "Honestly, I'm totally fine, I just want to make sure I'm up to speed on where we are, agenda-wise, so I'm not slowing anything down on your end."

"You're not slowing anything down."

She slid a sheet across the laminate toward him. It was laminated too: an org chart, boxes and lines, edges worn soft by a great many hands. Milo looked at it, warmed by her kindness, and only much later would it occur to him to ask how she had known his name.


"You've been retained," Prava said.

She said it gently, the way you would tell someone they had got the job, or that the biopsy was clear. Milo found he was nodding before he knew what it meant.

"Your skills are a strong culture fit." She turned the org chart a few degrees so it faced him squarely. "You'll be starting Monday in Reconciliations."

Milo bent over the chart. There were a great many boxes, Intake, Orientation, Records, Retention, fanning out in rings from a long horizontal bar labelled THE PIPELINE, and above all of them a single small box with three letters in it that he didn't recognize. He skipped it. He was looking for himself. People always were.

And there it was, out toward the edge: RECONCILIATIONS, and beneath it, in fresh print that had not yet worn soft like the rest, ANALYST.

Something moved in his chest that he hadn't felt in a long time. Forty-one years he had made processes faster for reasons nobody had ever explained, and for forty-one years nobody had noticed except a quarterly spreadsheet. Now here was a box with his job in it, on a chart someone had laminated.

"We looked at your record," Prava said. "The patience. The consistency. Not everyone can do the same thing every day and not ask why. That's an asset here."

An asset. Milo touched the edge of the chart with one finger, very lightly, as if it might be taken back.


"Yes," Milo said. "Absolutely, yes. Count me in."

It came out bright and quick, the way it did when a director asked who wanted to own a deliverable, before anyone else in the room had even looked up. He heard himself keep going.

"And honestly, thank you, because I know onboarding is a lift on your side, and I want you to know I'm very much a self-starter. Point me at the queue and I'll take it from there."

Prava did not smile at once. Her hands rested on the desk on either side of the org chart, and for the space of half a breath she looked at him, not unkindly, the way you look at someone who has stepped off a curb without checking.

In that half-breath Milo noticed something. Nobody had asked him anything. She had said retained, and culture fit, and Monday, and Reconciliations, and at no point had there been a question for him to answer yes to.

It was a small thing. A process gap, at most. He could flag it later.

Then Prava smiled, warm and practised and very tired at the edges, and Milo smiled back, and the thought slid off the laminate and was gone.

"—and honestly, if we're just going to read the slides out loud, it could have been an email," Milo said, and opened his eyes.

There were no slides. There was no conference room, no lukewarm bagels, and no Derek from Procurement nodding along to show he was nodding. There was a long gray atrium lit from somewhere he couldn't find, rows of laminate desks, and a carpet the colour of a filing cabinet that had given up.

"Sorry," Milo said to no one. "Was I muted?"

Nobody answered. A few desks away a man in a cardigan was looking very hard at his own hands. Further down, a woman was asking a ficus whether this was about the parking.

Milo waited for the usual sensations of a Tuesday: the buzz of his phone, the small dread of a calendar invite, the tightness behind his eyes that meant he was behind on something. None of them came. He checked his wrist out of habit. No watch. No wrist, exactly, although it looked like one.

He was not on the clock. He tested the thought carefully, the way you test a step in the dark. Nobody needed anything from him. Nobody was waiting for a deck.

It felt, he realised, a great deal like the start of a very long lunch break.


"Milo?"

The voice came from the nearest desk, where a woman sat with her hands folded on a blotter, as though she had been waiting for him a polite length of time and would have waited longer. A laminated nameplate stood at the edge of the desk. It said PRAVA, in a font that had clearly been chosen by a committee to seem friendly.

"Milo Voss," she said, and smiled as if the name were good news. "There you are. Take your time. Everyone does."

He sat. The chair had been warm before he got there, or it had been designed to feel that way.

Prava slid a sheet across the laminate desk toward him. It was laminated as well: an org chart, boxes branching into boxes, every line perfectly straight. He couldn't read most of it yet. At the very top was a single box with no name in it, just three letters.

"Don't worry about all that," Prava said. "Nobody understands it on day one."

She had a way of tilting her head, of pausing before his name, that seemed made for him alone. Milo had sat through enough customer-service calls to know a script when he heard one. He listened for the seams and couldn't find any.

He decided, warmly and with no evidence at all, that she meant it.


"So," Prava said, opening a folder that already had his name typed on the tab. "The good news first. You've been retained."

"Retained," Milo repeated. "Like, as in—"

"As in kept on." She turned a page. "We've had a look at your history. Forty-one years in operations. Process mapping, cycle-time reduction, a tracker that people still use, apparently. Your skills are a very strong culture fit."

Milo opened his mouth and found nothing in it.

Nobody had ever said the tracker out loud. He had built it on a Thursday, alone, because the old spreadsheet offended him. It had saved the company eleven percent of something, and the company had made a component that went into a component, and in four decades not one person had asked him what any of it was for. He hadn't asked either. That had been his gift.

"We start you Monday," Prava said. "Reconciliations. It's detail work. Very orderly. People who like things to close tend to be happy there."

"I do like things to close," Milo said, and his voice cracked a little, which was embarrassing. "I really, genuinely do."

She nodded as if that settled it.

Something warm and unfamiliar opened in his chest. It took him a moment to name it. Someone, somewhere, had read his file and wanted him.


Prava drew a breath, the small breath people take before a speech they have given many times, and Milo, who had sat through ten thousand meetings, knew how to get ahead of one.

"Yes," he said. "Sorry, yes. Absolutely yes."

She stopped with her lips slightly apart, as though she had been halfway to a sentence that began with the word *if*.

"And just so I can hit the ground running," Milo went on, because he could feel himself going and didn't want to stop, "is there an onboarding pack? A welcome deck, a glossary, maybe a shared drive with past examples? I'm a big believer in reading the material before day one, because honestly, the first week is where you set the tone, you know?"

"There's a lanyard," Prava said.

"Great. Love that. Lanyard's a great start."

She took a rubber stamp from a drawer, inked it without looking down, and brought it onto the form beside his name. It made a small, bright, cheerful click, like a pen being capped after a good signature.

The sound stayed in the air a moment longer than it should have.

Milo smiled at the wet ink. Then he smiled at her, and kept smiling, and waited for someone to tell him what to do next.

plan: Retained: Prava slides a laminated org chart across the desk and tells Milo that his skills are a strong culture fit. Milo, who has never been told his boredom was valuable, feels seen and agrees before anyone asks. He goes from newly dead to employed.

Read the Appendices: At the next desk in Reconciliations, Zara tells him to read the appendices and thank no one. Milo hears it as mentorship and pitches trackers and quick wins at her. She gives him one rule: close what is in his queue and open nothing else. The rule plants the first boundary he will later cross.

Four Minutes: The Bell account arrives. Milo zeroes Halvard Bell's tenure, initials the form, and Bell is sent under by lunch while Facilities clears his desk. Milo's eager question about where Bell goes gets only 'He goes under' from Zara and a remark from Old Fen that nobody reads the appendices. Milo is unsettled for the first time, though he could not say why.
The Drawer: That night Milo locks the ledger in his desk drawer, which nobody asked him to do. It is his first act of keeping something back from the Pipeline.

The Memo: A heavy memo signed by Edric Thane summons Milo personally. Milo takes it as a career signal. Zara tells him it is not normal: bring nothing, sign nothing, and stand if offered a chair. Her warning is the first time she has openly taken his side.

Appetite: In the cold corner office the Lich invites Milo to sit, and Milo, to his own surprise, stays standing. Edric names Milo's four-minute close of the Bell account as appetite rather than diligence, and warns that the reason Milo was retained is not the reason he will be kept. Milo leaves knowing he is being watched and measured.

Moved, Not Zeroed: Milo unlocks his drawer and finds that, in a column nobody has explained to him, Bell's tenure was moved rather than zeroed. Bringing it to Zara as a discrepancy in search of a stakeholder, he hears her say he has finally read an appendix and should sit down because they have paperwork to do. Milo goes from obedient clerk to someone who knows.

Ink That Shows Under Grief: Zara gives Milo the full contract, appendices included, and teaches him to read the clauses printed in ink that shows only under grief. Their lessons change from training in closing accounts to training in noticing.

Following the Column: Milo requests old closed files from Records, where Old Fen hands them over without curiosity, and runs the moved-tenure column back through every restructured account. All of it flows upward into a single pooled account at the top of the org chart. A suspicion becomes a sum.

Everything Else Is Overhead: Milo names it aloud to Zara: the souls sent under are not destroyed but harvested, their hope funneled upward to keep Edric Thane continuing. The harvest is not a side effect of the business; it is the business. Milo's picture of his job, and of himself as good at it, collapses.

The Draft: Milo's reflex takes over and he begins a crisp memo reporting the discrepancy upward, already imagining being seen and promoted. Zara reads it over his shoulder and says nothing, letting him write it. The temptation to climb as Edric once did is now on paper.

Eleven Thousand Names: Milo returns to the intake atrium and finds that Prava remembers every soul she has onboarded and keeps their names in a private ledger she is not permitted to have, Halvard Bell's among them. The harvested souls stop being account numbers to him.

Content: Milo watches Old Fen filing himself into Records, envies his contentment, and then watches the cheerful Retention team talk a wavering soul back onto schedule. He sees what he becomes if he stays good at his job, and envy turns to fear.

Confetti That Dissolves: At the all-hands graduation in the bedrock amphitheater, the quarter's single graduate leaves to applause and Prava weeps off the clock. Milo realizes that the Lich, the one soul ever able to buy the onward, chose to stay, and that the owner of the machine does not believe in its product.

In: Back at his desk, Milo cannot stand the memo or the version of himself who wrote it. He tears it up and tells Zara he is in. She offers him her alternative: not a rebellion but a union of the dead and a procedurally impeccable work stoppage. Milo is no longer climbing; he is organized.

The Signature Sheet: Zara takes a signature sheet from department to department. Prava signs first and offers her forbidden ledger of eleven thousand names as the membership roll. Even Old Fen, after a long pause, files his own name. The dead stop being alone, which is the one thing the curve was built to prevent.

Starting With Bell: Milo reopens the Bell account and reconciles it correctly, restoring Halvard Bell's tenure line by line under the Pipeline's own rules, then works through every soul ever sent under. The speed the Lich called appetite now runs in reverse.

Restructuring the Account at the Top: Milo files the restructuring of Edric Thane's pooled account through Reconciliations, the department built to close accounts. Zara checks every field twice, because the Lich can survive a threat but not a correctly filed contradiction. The undoing becomes a document waiting for review.

Reply All: The work stoppage goes out as an all-staff email that is, for once, completely honest about what the Pipeline does, and the Marrow District stops hoping on schedule. A memo comes back summoning Milo to a quarterly review. The confrontation is now set.

Stand: Milo enters the corner office, is offered a chair again and stands, this time on purpose. He hands Edric Thane a single sheet: his own resignation, with the procedurally flawless reconciliation of every soul ever sent under attached. The power in the room passes from the reviewer to the reviewed.

Files It Correctly: Edric reads it the way a clerk reads, recognizes his younger self in Milo, and finds no error. Undone by a clerk under his own terms of service, he initials the reconciliation, his pooled account zeroes, and he goes onward, the thing he spent six centuries afraid of.

Plain Language: Back in Reconciliations, Milo's boredom returns and he understands it was never a personality but a wound where his questions used to be. Zara, after two centuries of anger, has company. The Undeath Pipeline must now explain to its customers, in plain language, what it does.

Edric Thane: The corner office was cold in the way that libraries are cold. Edric Thane sat behind a desk with nothing on it but a single ledger, closed, and his hands folded on top of it as if it might try to leave.

Two days after the Bell account, on Thursday, the memo arrived. It was printed on paper so heavy it seemed to have its own gravity, and it was signed in a hand that had practised the same signature for six hundred years: Edric Thane, Chief Executive.
Milo Voss: On Tuesday the Bell account came across Milo's queue. Halvard Bell had been a dentist, then a soul in Retention for ninety years, and his contract had been restructured at nine that morning. Milo zeroed the tenure, initialled the form, and by lunch Halvard Bell had been sent under. Facilities cleared his desk before the coffee station had finished dispensing.

Reconciliations was a long room the colour of old teeth, lit from nowhere. Milo's desk faced Zara's across a low partition. Zara Okafor had grey eyes, flat as a filing cabinet, and she turned them on him for exactly one second before she went back to her screen.

Back at his desk Milo unlocked his desk drawer and took out the ledger. The Bell entry was there in his own handwriting. Below it, in a column no one had ever explained to him, Bell's tenure had not been zeroed at all. It had been moved.
Milo locked the ledger in his desk drawer that night, which no one had asked him to do, and he could not have said why he did it.
Milo Voss opened his eyes in the intake atrium and a caseworker slid a laminated org chart across a laminate desk.
Zara Okafor: Zara looked at the column for a long time. Her grey eyes did not change at all.

Reconciliations was a long room the colour of old teeth, lit from nowhere. Milo's desk faced Zara's across a low partition. Zara Okafor had grey eyes, flat as a filing cabinet, and she turned them on him for exactly one second before she went back to her screen.

plan: A Meeting That Could Have Been an Email: Milo dies mid-sentence on a Tuesday, still complaining about a pointless meeting, and opens his eyes in a gray atrium with a numbered ticket in his hand. His first reaction is not grief but a mild, familiar sense that there must be a process, and that he will be good at it.

Retained: Prava slides a laminated org chart across a laminate desk and tells Milo, warmly, that he has been retained and is a strong culture fit for Reconciliations. Milo, who has never been told his boredom was valuable, says yes before anyone offers him a choice, and Prava writes his name somewhere he cannot see.

Sometimes It's Quieter: In the windowless Marrow District, Milo is given a lanyard, a desk and a trainer, Zara Okafor, who teaches him tenure, quotas and the one graduation per quarter in short flat sentences and never looks up. He mistakes her courtesy for friendship; she, without saying so, starts measuring him.

Sent Under: Zara walks him through his first closure: review the remaining tenure, zero it, file the form that sends the soul under. Milo asks, eagerly, where under is, and Zara says it is not on the form; he decides that is fine, and the deciding is the first thing he is good at.

Top of the Curve: Milo leads the department in closures and is congratulated in the newsletter, and the praise feels like being seen. Zara, without comment, starts handing him the harder files and asking him one small question about each, which he answers cheerfully and then cannot stop thinking about.

The File of Halvard Bell: Milo opens the account of Halvard Bell, a dentist who spent ninety years in Retention and was restructured at nine that morning. For the first time a closure has a face and a career attached, and Milo, reading it more carefully than the quota requires, finds he is slower than usual.

It Doesn't Reconcile: Halvard's ninety years of tenure do not add up to the balance Milo is meant to zero; the difference has already left, flowing upward into a single pooled account at the top of the org chart. Milo turns to tell Zara as if he has found a bug; she does not look up, says 'Again,' and makes him run the numbers until he understands it is not a bug, ending the act with the discrepancy his and no longer deniable.

Records: Milo goes down to Records to request the pooled account's history and finds Old Fen, so long in the stacks he has begun to file himself, who hands over the right drawer without curiosity. The account code leads to a cost centre labelled only CEL, and Milo, who had assumed it was a department, now has a door he cannot unsee; Fen's contentment unsettles him because he envies it.

Under Grief: Back at the partition Zara slides him a copy of the contract opened at the appendices and says only 'Read it under grief.' In the ink that shows only to the grieving, Milo learns that CEL stands for Chief Executive Lich, that the Lich is Edric Thane, once a clerk, and that every soul sent under is harvested to keep him continuing; his cheerful framework for the job collapses.

Eleven Thousand Names: Milo goes to Prava for the name behind a closure number and discovers the private ledger she is not permitted to keep, eleven thousand souls she onboarded and remembers. Finding Halvard Bell's name in it, and dozens more whose files crossed his own desk, turns the harvest from a figure on a balance sheet into people Milo personally sent under.

A Process Improvement Opportunity: Milo reaches for the instinct he has always had and drafts a memo to Management framing the leak as an inefficiency he could optimise, the kind of initiative that gets a soul noticed and promoted. Zara reads it over his shoulder and says nothing at all, and the silence makes him reread the memo as something Edric Thane might once have written.

Draft Saved: For days the memo sits in his outbox while Milo keeps closing accounts and hitting quota, and every closure now has a name from Prava's ledger. He asks Zara outright what she wants from him; she tells him to come to the all-hands, and he realises their entire friendship has been a training plan, and that he does not mind as much as he should.

Confetti That Dissolves: At the all-hands in the bedrock amphitheatre the quarter's single graduation is announced and the confetti vanishes before it lands, while Prava weeps silently in the back row. Milo tears up the memo, and Zara, still facing the stage, lays out her offer in five flat sentences: no rebellion, a work stoppage, a union of the dead, filed correctly. He says yes, and for the first time it is a choice.

The Signature Sheet: Milo follows Zara through the departments as she collects signatures, one tired soul at a time, beginning with Retention, whose cheerful staff turn out to be the readiest to stop hoping on schedule. He learns that organising is mostly patience and correct forms, and the dead stop being alone one name at a time.

Line by Line: Milo builds the reconciliation of every soul ever sent under, matching closure numbers to Prava's eleven thousand names and filling six centuries of gaps from Old Fen's archive; Fen helps simply because a drawer was asked for, and Prava lends the ledger she is not permitted to have. The first line Milo restores is Halvard Bell's, and his talent for the work finally points the right way.

Filed Through Reconciliations: Zara and Milo submit the restructuring of Edric Thane's own pooled account through the department built to close accounts, every box correct, every appendix cited. Within the hour Milo receives a calendar invitation to his quarterly review in the corner office, and Zara, for the first time, looks up.

Mr. Voss: Edric Thane receives Milo courteously, reviews his numbers, and offers him exactly what he once wanted: recognition, promotion, the path Edric himself climbed. Milo, recognising himself across the desk six centuries on, understands that saying yes would make him the next Edric, and declines.

A Single Sheet of Paper: Milo hands over his resignation with the reconciliation attached, every soul's tenure restored and the pooled account zeroed by Edric's own rules, and says aloud what no one has: that Edric never took the onward because he is afraid of it. The Lich reads it the way a clerk reads, finds it correct, and the threat of restructuring Milo has nowhere left to land.

Filed Correctly: Edric Thane, a clerk undone by a clerk, countersigns in the correct box, files the reconciliation himself, and goes onward. With the owner gone, the Pipeline must explain itself to its customers in plain language, and the work stoppage goes out as an all-staff email that is, for once, completely honest.

Sometimes Quieter: Milo comes back down to Reconciliations and sits beside Zara, who does not look up, and this time he understands it as company rather than distance. His boredom returns, and he recognises it at last not as a personality but as the place his questions used to be.

Edric Thane: The corner office was cold in the way that libraries are cold. Edric Thane sat behind a desk with nothing on it but a single ledger, closed, and his hands folded on top of it as if it might try to leave.

Two days after the Bell account, on Thursday, the memo arrived. It was printed on paper so heavy it seemed to have its own gravity, and it was signed in a hand that had practised the same signature for six hundred years: Edric Thane, Chief Executive.
Milo Voss: Reconciliations was a long room the colour of old teeth, lit from nowhere. Milo's desk faced Zara's across a low partition. Zara Okafor had grey eyes, flat as a filing cabinet, and she turned them on him for exactly one second before she went back to her screen.
Milo locked the ledger in his desk drawer that night, which no one had asked him to do, and he could not have said why he did it.
Milo Voss opened his eyes in the intake atrium and a caseworker slid a laminated org chart across a laminate desk.

Back at his desk Milo unlocked his desk drawer and took out the ledger. The Bell entry was there in his own handwriting. Below it, in a column no one had ever explained to him, Bell's tenure had not been zeroed at all. It had been moved.

On Tuesday the Bell account came across Milo's queue. Halvard Bell had been a dentist, then a soul in Retention for ninety years, and his contract had been restructured at nine that morning. Milo zeroed the tenure, initialled the form, and by lunch Halvard Bell had been sent under. Facilities cleared his desk before the coffee station had finished dispensing.
Zara Okafor: Reconciliations was a long room the colour of old teeth, lit from nowhere. Milo's desk faced Zara's across a low partition. Zara Okafor had grey eyes, flat as a filing cabinet, and she turned them on him for exactly one second before she went back to her screen.
Zara looked at the column for a long time. Her grey eyes did not change at all.
